title: The Final Walk
tagline: You return to the hall where it began, and walk the whole house once, from the front door to the great hall.
card: A last walk through all thirty rooms: what you have, what to use it for, and a test that mixes everything.
goal: you will walk through the whole course, test yourself on a mixed set of questions from every wing, and make a plan for the next thirty days.

left_off.q: What is the best size for a daily practice session?
left_off.a: About twenty minutes: warm-up, review, new work and a log.

left_off.q: When do you review a new set?
left_off.a: After one day, three days, a week, two weeks and a month.

left_off.q: What grew in S.F. over eighteen months?
left_off.a: A skill, not his general memory.

text: Imagine you are standing in the doorway of a great hall. It is a still morning. The roof is whole, the columns are tall, and the long tables are laid for a banquet that will never happen. It is the hall from the oldest story in this course, where a poet once stood in the door and a roof fell behind him.

You are not here to mourn. You are here to walk. Because that is what the poet did, and what this whole course has taught you to do. Order and place. If you can walk through a place, you can walk through anything you have put in it.

check.q: What did the poet's story teach at the beginning of the course?
check.a: That remembering where things are, in a place we know, lets us recall them in order.

parts.talk: What is the most surprising thing you have learned about your own memory in this course?

text: You begin at the front door, where you learned how memory works and how a picture sticks. You pass the body, the building and the chain. You cross into the counting house, where numbers became pictures, then people, then scenes. You enter the market square, with its names, cards, talks and maps. You climb to the library, with its words, verbs, lists and formulas.

Then the tower, where you learned to go fast, to keep dates, to pack three digits into a syllable, to join palaces, and to give ideas a body. And finally the great hall, with its speeches, its books, its competitions, its habits. It is a long walk, and you have taken it.

check.q: Name the six wings of the house in order.
check.a: The Front Door, the Counting House, the Market Square, the Library, the Tower, the Great Hall.

parts.talk: Which wing was your favourite? Which would you like to go back to?

text: A last word, as old as the first. The Roman teachers said that memory is a treasure-house of ideas. A house is no use unless you live in it. What you have now is a method, and a method grows with use.

So this last room has three jobs. To walk the whole house once. To test you on a mixture of everything. And to help you plan what to do in the next thirty days, so that what you have learned becomes a habit.

check.q: What are the three jobs of this room?
check.a: To walk the whole house, test you on everything, and plan the next thirty days.

items: Week 1: a twenty-minute session each day, with one palace.
Week 2: add a second tool: names, numbers or a talk.
Week 3: a weekly test with at least three kinds of material.
Week 4: teach someone one of the methods.
At day 30: come back to this room, walk the house, and see what has stayed.

method.x: Walk the six wings aloud, naming at least two tools in each.

try.title: Your thirty-day plan
try.prompt: Write a thirty-day plan: what you will practise each week, for how long each day, and how you will log it.
try.model: Week 1: 20 minutes daily, one palace of ten places and ten words. Week 2: add names. Week 3: a weekly test of words, faces and numbers. Week 4: teach a friend the Major System. Log in a notebook. Day 30: review.
checks: There is a plan for each of four weeks.
